questions.explanation: Raw secret-prefix hashes allow extension forgeries by state continuation. HMAC double-dips with inner and outer pads to kill that class.

questions.question: In which order do the TCP server calls run for one listening socket?
options: socket, bind, listen, then loop accept, recv, send, close per client
connect, bind, listen, then accept once for all clients
socket, connect, sendto, recvfrom with no listen
bind, socket, accept, then listen after each close
questions.answer: socket, bind, listen, then loop accept, recv, send, close per client
questions.explanation: The listening socket only births connected sockets via accept; each child talks to exactly one client while the parent keeps ringing.

questions.question: select overwrites its fd_sets, so they must be rebuilt before every call.
questions.explanation: The returned sets are results, not reusable watchlists; reuse misreports readiness and stalls the loop.

questions.question: Residuals are [2, -2, 0, 4]. What are MAE and RMSE, and why does RMSE exceed MAE?
options: MAE 2.0 and RMSE about 2.45, because squaring over-weights the 4
MAE 8.0 and RMSE 6.0, because sums beat means
MAE 2.45 and RMSE 2.0, because roots shrink large misses
MAE and RMSE are always identical on any residuals
questions.answer: MAE 2.0 and RMSE about 2.45, because squaring over-weights the 4
questions.explanation: MAE averages misses while RMSE averages squares then roots, so the lone large miss dominates and the gap measures outlier spread.

questions.question: RIDGE keeps all features with dense shrinkage while LASSO can pin weak weights exactly to zero.
questions.explanation: L2 shrinks smoothly with a closed form; L1 corners select sparsely with no closed form.

questions.question: TP 12, FP 3, FN 8, TN 77. What are precision, recall, and F1?
options: Precision 0.80, recall 0.60, F1 about 0.69
Precision 0.60, recall 0.80, F1 about 0.69
Precision 0.89, recall 0.89, F1 0.89
Precision 0.12, recall 0.08, F1 about 0.10
questions.answer: Precision 0.80, recall 0.60, F1 about 0.69
questions.explanation: Precision audits the predicted-positive column 12/15; recall audits the actual-positive row 12/20; F1 harmonically compromises at about 0.69.

questions.question: AUC grades ranking across all thresholds, so the deployed threshold still needs its own precision and recall report.
questions.explanation: A higher area can hide a worse operating dot; ship the dot the cost chose, ranked by the area.

questions.question: What separates a microcontroller from a microprocessor?
options: A microcontroller holds CPU, RAM, ROM and I/O on one chip; a microprocessor holds only the CPU
A microprocessor holds everything on-chip; a microcontroller holds only the CPU
Both are identical except for the brand name
Microcontrollers always run a full operating system
questions.answer: A microcontroller holds CPU, RAM, ROM and I/O on one chip; a microprocessor holds only the CPU
questions.explanation: Correct: integration decides — the all-in-one chip runs fixed firmware jobs while the CPU-only chip needs external support. The distractors invert the definitions, claim identity, or drag in operating systems that define purpose, not construction.

questions.question: A TV remote uses a microcontroller because it runs one fixed job within tight power and cost limits.
questions.explanation: Correct: fixed single purpose plus power and cost limits point to the all-in-one chip. A laptop fails the test on every axis — general software under an OS with external memory.

questions.question: How do you set pin 5 of a port without disturbing other pins?
options: REG ^= 0xFF
questions.explanation: Correct: OR pastes a 1 on while zeros pass through untouched. Assignment wipes the rest, AND reads rather than writes, and XOR with 0xFF flips everything instead of one pin.

questions.question: Every memory-mapped register and every variable shared with an ISR must be volatile.
questions.explanation: Correct: hardware and interrupts change memory behind the program's back, so volatile forces a fresh read every time. Without it, release optimisation caches the first read forever.

questions.question: What does ARM sell to chip makers like STMicroelectronics?
options: Processor blueprints and core designs under license; licensees build the chips
Finished STM32 chips ready for sale
Only software tools and debuggers
Silicon wafers and packaging services
questions.answer: Processor blueprints and core designs under license; licensees build the chips
questions.explanation: Correct: ARM designs and licenses cores and architectures but fabricates no chips — ST builds STM32s around licensed cores. Any option naming ARM as a chip maker collapses licensor into manufacturer.

questions.question: On ARM, arithmetic instructions work only on registers; only LDR and STR touch memory.
questions.explanation: Correct: the load-store law forbids memory operands in arithmetic, so memory-arithmetic C lines compile to load-add-store triples. A single memory-arithmetic instruction cannot exist on ARM.

questions.question: What does Armv8-M add over ARMv7-M that a compare-generations answer must list?
options: TrustZone worlds, hardware stack-limit checking, improved exception handling, authenticated debug
Higher Megahertz and a lower price only
Thumb-2 instruction encoding
A built-in operating system
questions.answer: TrustZone worlds, hardware stack-limit checking, improved exception handling, authenticated debug
questions.explanation: Correct: generations differ by architecture features — worlds, stack limits, exceptions, debug auth. Megahertz, price, or logos never appear in a generation comparison answer.

questions.question: Non-secure code calling into the Secure world must enter through Non-secure-Callable veneers; direct calls fault.
questions.explanation: Correct: only callable veneers are legal gates, so skipping one faults by design. The fault proves the border holds against exactly this shortcut.

questions.question: A firmware write targets address 0x48000014. What happens, and why?
options: It drives a peripheral register (0x48 is peripheral space), moving hardware, not memory
It stores a variable in SRAM like any other address
It executes code from flash
Addresses are decorative; nothing happens
questions.answer: It drives a peripheral register (0x48 is peripheral space), moving hardware, not memory
questions.explanation: Correct: load/store is district-blind, so the 0x48 prefix means hardware levers while 0x20 means SRAM data. Treating all addresses as memory misses the map's whole job.

questions.question: On Cortex-M the stack grows toward lower addresses and overflow eats heap and variables below.
questions.explanation: Correct: descent has no brakes without limits, and overflow eats heap and variables below. Armv8-M stack limits convert silent corruption into a catchable fault.

questions.question: What does the U in STM32U575 tell you, and which chip suits a battery sensor needing TrustZone?
options: Ultra-low-power mission; the U575, which pairs coin-cell sleep currents with a TrustZone-capable M33
USB support; any F-series chip instead
U stands for untested silicon
The letter is random marketing
questions.answer: Ultra-low-power mission; the U575, which pairs coin-cell sleep currents with a TrustZone-capable M33
questions.explanation: Correct: the series letter names the mission, and battery plus TrustZone pick U5's 575 line. F-series answers mains-powered mainstream jobs, not coin-cell vaults.

questions.question: HAL GPIO code ports across STM32 series for core logic, but clocks, power modes and security setup must be redone per chip.
questions.explanation: Correct: shared chassis transfers habits while clocks, power, and security stay chip-specific. Expecting binary portability ignores the reference-manual halves.

questions.question: A node is awake 1 s hourly at 10 mA and sleeps at 1 microamp. What dominates battery life?
options: Sleep current, because it rules 99.9% of the time: average is about 3.8 microamps
Active current, because milliamps dwarf microamps
The clock speed during sleep
The LED brightness setting
questions.answer: Sleep current, because it rules 99.9% of the time: average is about 3.8 microamps
questions.explanation: Correct: the charge-weighted mean is ruled by the 99.9% sleep term. Active-current comparisons without duty cycles compare sprints while batteries die in sleep.

questions.question: Entering Stop mode without enabling a wake-up source leaves the chip unreachable until reset.
questions.explanation: Correct: deep sleep with no wired wake source is absence until reset. Debugging sleep starts at the wire, never at the depth.

questions.question: GPIO writes do nothing on a fresh STM32 program. What is the first fix?
options: Enable the port's peripheral clock before configuring pins
Increase the delay loop
Rewrite the code in assembly
Replace the microcontroller
questions.answer: Enable the port's peripheral clock before configuring pins
questions.explanation: Correct: gated-off peripherals ignore writes silently, so clock-enable precedes all configuration. Rewriting code or blaming silicon skips the power-physics step.

questions.question: Reset leaves STM32 pins as analog inputs, so every used pin needs an explicit mode setup.
questions.explanation: Correct: reset leaves pins as analog inputs for lowest power. Every used pin needs explicit mode setup — the most common dead-LED cause.

questions.question: Four multiplexed digits flicker visibly. What does the 2 ms-per-digit arithmetic say?
options: Total refresh must stay near 8 ms (125 Hz); flicker means slices too long, so quicken each digit slot
Add more digits to share the load
Multiplexing always flickers and cannot be fixed
Slow the loop for stability
questions.answer: Total refresh must stay near 8 ms (125 Hz); flicker means slices too long, so quicken each digit slot
questions.explanation: Correct: total refresh must stay near 8 ms, so flicker means overlong slices. More digits or slower loops worsen both failure modes instead of fixing them.

questions.question: An LCD prints commands as actions (jumps and clears) instead of text because data was sent with RS=0.
questions.explanation: Correct: RS selects meaning on shared wires — 0 commands, 1 prints. Rewriting init misses that identical bytes behave differently per RS.

questions.question: A 12-bit ADC with 3.3 V reference reads 1.65 V. What code results?
options: About 2047, since code equals input over reference times 4095
About 4095 regardless of input
About 1024 always at mid-supply
Zero, because mid-supply is undefined
questions.answer: About 2047, since code equals input over reference times 4095
questions.explanation: Correct: half of reference gives half of 4095. Saturation options ignore the linear ruler; mid-supply is the most defined point, not an edge case.

questions.question: PWM average voltage equals duty share times supply, so duty (not frequency) carries LED and servo meaning.
questions.explanation: Correct: duty is the message and frequency only needs to exceed perception. Reading frequency as meaning inverts the PWM contract.

questions.question: What transfer rate do user bytes achieve on 115200 baud 8N1, and why?
options: About 11520 bytes/s, because each byte costs 10 frame bits including start and stop
115200 bytes/s, since baud equals bytes
About 1152 bytes/s, since parity doubles the cost
Baud rates are unrelated to byte rates
questions.answer: About 11520 bytes/s, because each byte costs 10 frame bits including start and stop
questions.explanation: Correct: baud counts framing bits, so 8N1 divides by 10 first. Equating baud with bytes overstates speed tenfold.

questions.question: A parity bit detects single-bit flips but never corrects errors.
questions.explanation: Correct: parity flags single-bit flips and corrects nothing. Correction needs codes above this layer.

questions.question: A terminal garbles right after firmware doubles the PLL clock with nothing else changed. What is wrong?
options: The baud divisor went stale: actual baud doubled with the clock, so recompute it
Parity must now be enabled to compensate
GPIO pins melted from the higher speed
USART peripherals cannot run above 40 MHz
questions.answer: The baud divisor went stale: actual baud doubled with the clock, so recompute it
questions.explanation: Correct: baud is a ratio with the clock, so doubling the clock doubles actual baud until the divisor is recomputed. Parity, pins, and speed caps are unrelated suspects.

questions.question: Polling suits single bytes while interrupt-driven ring buffers suit streams, because polling holds the whole CPU per byte.
questions.explanation: Correct: polling rents the whole CPU per byte-time while interrupts rent microseconds. Volume decides the architecture — streams demand buffers.

questions.question: An I2C master addresses 0x48 for writing and gets NACK. What should be checked first?
options: Whether any slave owns 0x48, whether it is powered, and whether pull-ups exist
The CPU clock speed setting
Whether the LCD contrast is adjusted
The USB cable version
questions.answer: Whether any slave owns 0x48, whether it is powered, and whether pull-ups exist
questions.explanation: Correct: address-phase NACK reports absence in debug order — identity, power, then physics. Slowing clocks or sending STOPs addresses no cause.

questions.question: I2C lines are open-drain, so missing pull-up resistors leave the whole bus dead.
questions.explanation: Correct: open-drain devices pull low only, so resistors restore high. Without them the bus never rises and every transaction fails identically.

questions.question: EEPROM writes clock perfectly on the bus but data vanishes after power-cycle. What step was skipped?
options: The WREN write-enable latch: transfers clocked fine but cells never burned without it
The SPI clock speed setting
The chip-select polarity jumper
The parity configuration
questions.answer: The WREN write-enable latch: transfers clocked fine but cells never burned without it
questions.explanation: Correct: the WREN latch bridges transfer and storage — bus success without it is theatre with correct timing. Speed, polarity, and parity never gate storage.

questions.question: A multi-byte EEPROM write must never cross a page boundary in one operation, because addresses wrap within the page.
questions.explanation: Correct: addresses wrap within the page, so crossing writes tear head and tail. Page math (fill, wholes, remainder) precedes every multi-byte write.

questions.question: Two CAN nodes with IDs 0x100 and 0x180 start together. What happens?
options: 0x100 wins at the first bit where it drives dominant 0 against 0x180's recessive 1; the loser backs off and retries
0x180 wins because higher numbers have seniority
Both frames merge into 0x180
A master chip referees the collision
questions.answer: 0x100 wins at the first bit where it drives dominant 0 against 0x180's recessive 1; the loser backs off and retries
questions.explanation: Correct: wired-AND decides mid-bit with lower winning gracefully and the frame intact. Seniority, merging, and referee chips misunderstand the mechanism.

questions.question: USB HID lets a sensor gadget work with no custom PC driver by disguising as a keyboard or joystick through report descriptors.
questions.explanation: Correct: standard classes bring built-in OS drivers, so descriptors declare identity without installs. Custom classes would need the forbidden drivers.

questions.question: One thousand sensors stream telemetry to dashboards and a rule engine. Why MQTT over CoAP?
options: Publishers file once to a broker that fans out to all subscribers, instead of thousands of direct query relationships
CoAP cannot use UDP
MQTT is always faster for single queries
Brokers are unnecessary overhead
questions.answer: Publishers file once to a broker that fans out to all subscribers, instead of thousands of direct query relationships
questions.explanation: Correct: one publish fans out to all subscribers, replacing thousands of direct query relationships. Raw sockets or CoAP-per-dashboard rebuild the coupling the broker removes.

questions.question: QoS 0 suits expendable telemetry while QoS 2 suits actuation where duplicates corrupt, because QoS prices duplicate tolerance.
questions.explanation: Correct: QoS prices duplicate tolerance per flow — telemetry tolerates loss, actuation cannot tolerate doubles. Maximum-everywhere wastes handshakes; anxiety is not a level.

questions.question: A 3 km soil probe reporting hourly on battery needs which radio, and why?
options: LoRa, for kilometre range with byte rates under duty caps that allow years of battery
Bluetooth, for the longest range
GSM for the lowest power
Wi-Fi for kilometre penetration
questions.answer: LoRa, for kilometre range with byte rates under duty caps that allow years of battery
questions.explanation: Correct: kilometres plus byte rates plus duty-capped battery is LoRa's exact triangle seat. Bluetooth fails range, GSM fails power, Wi-Fi fails both.

questions.question: Recorded unlock commands replayed later are defeated by nonces or monotonic counters, not by encryption alone.
questions.explanation: Correct: authentication answers identity while freshness answers time — encryption without nonces still replays. Each attack row needs its own cure.

questions.question: Adding a display routine to a super-loop makes braking miss deadlines. Why does an RTOS fix this structurally?
options: Loop timing sums all code before each job, while the scheduler preempts by priority, bounding urgent latency
An RTOS runs code at higher Megahertz
An RTOS deletes low-priority tasks automatically
Deadlines do not apply to scheduled systems
questions.answer: Loop timing sums all code before each job, while the scheduler preempts by priority, bounding urgent latency
questions.explanation: Correct: loop latency couples every job to every other while scheduler latency couples each job only to higher priorities. Megahertz never fixes structural coupling.

questions.question: A high task waiting on a mutex held by a low task while a medium task runs long is priority inversion, cured by priority inheritance.
questions.explanation: Correct: waiter, holder, and middle spoiler make inversion, and inheritance lends urgency to the holder. Raising the medium task or rebooting misdiagnoses the three-rung shape.

questions.question: Two tasks share one UART. Why must the guard be a mutex rather than a binary semaphore?
options: Only mutexes carry priority inheritance, so an urgent waiter lends urgency to the holder instead of suffering inversion
Binary semaphores are slower
Mutexes use less RAM
UARTs serialize themselves without guards
questions.answer: Only mutexes carry priority inheritance, so an urgent waiter lends urgency to the holder instead of suffering inversion
questions.explanation: Correct: only owned mutexes carry inheritance, defeating the wedge between holder and waiter. Lighter primitives reintroduce the exact cured hazard.

questions.question: ISRs may give semaphores and send to queues with FromISR forms, but must never take mutexes or block.
questions.explanation: Correct: bells ring but never hold meetings — blocking ISRs freeze everything below their priority. Mutexes and blocking calls belong to tasks only.

questions.question: Where do a door lock's PIN store and Bluetooth stack live under TrustZone, and how do they interact?
options: PIN store and checker in Secure; Bluetooth, LED and logs in Non-secure; crossings only via verify veneers
Everything in Secure for maximum safety
Everything in Non-secure since TrustZone is decorative
PIN in Non-secure flash protected by TLS
questions.answer: PIN store and checker in Secure; Bluetooth, LED and logs in Non-secure; crossings only via verify veneers
questions.explanation: Correct: minimal vault stays auditable — secrets plus checkers inside, replaceable code outside, yes-or-no veneers between. All-Secure fails auditability; Non-secure PINs fail everything.

questions.question: A two-year battery claim must be proved with duty-cycle average-current math, measured sleep current, and capacity division.
questions.explanation: Correct: formula plus measurement plus capacity plus margin, or the claim is decoration. Logos and retrofitted batteries are not evidence.

questions.question: Ping to 8.8.8.8 works but the browser fails everywhere. Which layer failed?
options: DNS name resolution, since IPs route fine while names never resolve
The gateway cable
The DHCP lease
The browser installation
questions.answer: DNS name resolution, since IPs route fine while names never resolve
questions.explanation: Correct: working IPs with dead names isolate the resolver path — inspect resolv.conf and the DNS server's reachability. Cables, leases, and browsers are innocent when pings reply.

questions.question: An ss entry of 0.0.0.0:8080 means the program accepts connections on all interfaces, while 127.0.0.1 means loopback only.
questions.explanation: Correct: the pre-colon address names the audience — all-interfaces serves the LAN, loopback serves self. Rebinding, not firewall lore, fixes reachability asymmetry.

questions.question: A restarted TCP server fails with Errno 98 though old clients are gone. What lingers?
options: The old connection in TIME_WAIT holding the port; SO_REUSEADDR permits immediate rebind
A burnt port that can never be reused
A Python cache of port numbers
A loopback policy needing root
questions.answer: The old connection in TIME_WAIT holding the port; SO_REUSEADDR permits immediate rebind
questions.explanation: Correct: TIME_WAIT guards late duplicates after close, and the socket option permits immediate rebind. Burnt ports, caches, and privilege theories mistake state for damage.

questions.question: When recv returns empty bytes, the peer has closed its side: it is TCP's hang-up notice, never data.
questions.explanation: Correct: reads return data, then zero bytes at orderly close — empty is the hang-up notice. Chasing speed or blaming loopback misses the protocol signal.

questions.question: A UDP client hangs forever on its first request while the server logs nothing. What is wrong?
options: The server is down or the port is wrong, and the client has no timeout: connectionless failure is silent
Python is too slow for UDP
UDP always needs connect first
Loopback blocks UDP by policy
questions.answer: The server is down or the port is wrong, and the client has no timeout: connectionless failure is silent
questions.explanation: Correct: connectionless failure is silent, so prove the server first and armor clients with timeouts. Speed, connect rituals, and loopback policies are non-causes.

questions.question: Blocking recvfrom with no timeout freezes forever on the first lost datagram, so UDP clients must set timeouts and plan retries.
questions.explanation: Correct: loss is normal on networks, so unbounded waits turn one drop into eternity. Timeouts plus retries are mandatory, not polite.

questions.question: An accepted socket is never added to the select watch set. What does its client see?
options: Connect then silence forever, since readable bytes on an unwatched descriptor are never reported
Faster service from fewer watched sockets
An immediate server crash
Automatic discovery by select
questions.answer: Connect then silence forever, since readable bytes on an unwatched descriptor are never reported
questions.explanation: Correct: the kernel reports only listed descriptors, so unwatched clients stay silent forever. Crashes, speedups, and auto-discovery contradict the watch invariant.

questions.question: Per-client line buffers plus reply-only-on-newline let complete requests jump ahead of a slow client's partial line.
questions.explanation: Correct: buffered lines plus readiness dispatch let complete work jump partial work. Threading claims and byte-reordering theories miss the actual fairness mechanism.

questions.question: A capture shows zero packets though the client printed its reply. What is wrong?
options: Wrong interface or an over-narrow capture filter: the working traffic alibis the packets, so the microscope is mispointed
Wireshark is broken and must be reinstalled
TCP hides from Wireshark by encryption
Loopback traffic cannot be captured
questions.answer: Wrong interface or an over-narrow capture filter: the working traffic alibis the packets, so the microscope is mispointed
questions.explanation: Correct: proven traffic alibis the packets, so the fault lies with interface or pre-Start filter. Reinstalls, encryption, and loopback myths blame the wrong layer.

questions.question: Capture filters decide what gets recorded before Start, while display filters decide what is viewed after, and their syntaxes differ.
questions.explanation: Correct: BPF records while display-language views — red means rejected syntax in the current box. Port numbers and colours are innocent; grammar is guilty.

questions.question: Under 15 percent loss the capture shows dup ACKs, a black retransmission, yet the client prints the full reply. What happened?
options: The receiver begged the gap with dup ACKs, the sender repaired it, and reassembly delivered ordered bytes
The reply was pure luck
Wireshark repairs packets itself
Retransmissions duplicate the reply text
questions.answer: The receiver begged the gap with dup ACKs, the sender repaired it, and reassembly delivered ordered bytes
questions.explanation: Correct: dups diagnose the gap, black resends cure it, identical bytes certify the repair loop. Luck, Wireshark magic, and duplication theories skip all three phases.

questions.question: A FIN close drains gracefully while an RST close aborts with in-flight data at risk.
questions.explanation: Correct: FIN drains gracefully while RST destroys with data at risk — asymmetry tells which side died mid-sentence. Speed and symmetry claims misread close semantics.

questions.question: DORA shows Discover, Offer and Request but no Ack, and the machine keeps 169.254.x.x. What happened?
options: The server never acknowledged, so the client fell back to link-local self-assignment with no gateway
The lease succeeded and 169.254 is the server address
Three DORA packets suffice for a lease
DHCP uses 169.254 as its server address
questions.answer: The server never acknowledged, so the client fell back to link-local self-assignment with no gateway
questions.explanation: Correct: four letters or no lease — 169.254 confesses a missing Ack via link-local fallback. Celebrating it or blaming three-packet sufficiency inverts the protocol.

questions.question: A repeated dig answering in 0 msec proves the answer came from cache, with TTL counting down.
questions.explanation: Correct: zero query time is the cache's signature with TTL counting down. Slow-lookup theories contradict the timing evidence.

questions.question: Go-Back-N with a 20 ms timeout on a 100 ms RTT link barely beats stop-and-wait. Why?
options: The timeout fires mid-flight every packet, resending healthy goods continuously: set two to four times the RTT
The window is too big and must shrink to one
Loss is too low to matter
Python is too slow for windows
questions.answer: The timeout fires mid-flight every packet, resending healthy goods continuously: set two to four times the RTT
questions.explanation: Correct: sub-RTT timeouts resend healthy goods continuously — kindness becomes congestion. Window size, loss levels, and language speed are unrelated suspects.

questions.question: A Go-Back-N receiver drops post-gap packets and keeps ACKing the gap, forcing the sender to rewind and resend from it.
questions.explanation: Correct: GBN receivers drop post-gap data and beg the gap, so senders rewind — simplicity priced as waste. Delivering gaps or manual resends violate the contract.

questions.question: Routes are perfect on both hosts, interfaces are up, yet pings fail through the router namespace. What is off?
options: IP forwarding in the router: tables name doors but the switch opens them
The veth cables are unplugged virtually
Ping is blocked by namespaces permanently
veth ends need their own IP addresses
questions.answer: IP forwarding in the router: tables name doors but the switch opens them
questions.explanation: Correct: tables name doors but the forwarding switch opens them — perfect tables with a dead switch fail identically to no tables. Cables, ping bans, and veth addressing miss the two-half diagnosis.

questions.question: Routing is per-direction state: a working forward path never implies the return path, so every path needs its mirror route.
questions.explanation: Correct: requests and replies route independently, so one working direction proves exactly half the tables. One-way forwarding and reply-exempt theories deny per-direction state.

questions.question: A public peer's new connection to a private server times out with zero replies. What hides the server?
options: NAT without a port-forward: inbound has no mapping, so nothing delivers; reachability needs an explicit DNAT rule
A firewall REJECT rule sending instant refusals
MASQUERADE blocking all TCP
Private servers cannot exist behind NAT
questions.answer: NAT without a port-forward: inbound has no mapping, so nothing delivers; reachability needs an explicit DNAT rule
questions.explanation: Correct: NAT hides by default with no mapping for inbound, and DROP adds silence — reachability needs explicit DNAT. REJECT, MASQUERADE-blame, and impossibility claims misread both layers.

questions.question: ESTABLISHED rules must come before default DROP so a gate's own answers can re-enter.
questions.explanation: Correct: replies are INPUT-path packets, so ESTABLISHED-first is self-preservation. New-only DROP theories forget the admin's own traffic obeys the rules.

questions.question: A simulation reports 8 Mbps on a 5 Mbps link. What is wrong?
options: Measurement accounting: throughput can never exceed the bottleneck, so recheck parsing against DataRate as a ceiling
The link overperforms and deserves a bonus report
ns-3 is optimistic by design
DataRate means something else in simulation
questions.answer: Measurement accounting: throughput can never exceed the bottleneck, so recheck parsing against DataRate as a ceiling
questions.explanation: Correct: throughput can never exceed the bottleneck, so impossible numbers indict measurement parsing first. Bonuses, optimism, and redefined DataRate deny physics.

questions.question: A sweep must change one parameter per curve with fixed seeds, or blame for any collapse is unassignable.
questions.explanation: Correct: two knobs turned means blame unassignable — one parameter per curve with fixed seeds is the causality contract. Collapse admiration and seed superstition skip experimental design.

questions.question: A DNAT rule exists yet the forwarded service times out externally while LAN access works. What is missing?
options: The matching FORWARD accept: translation and permission are separate verdicts, and LAN bypasses both
A VPN replacement for DNAT
Binding the service to the public IP directly
Timeouts indicate success in firewall logic
questions.answer: The matching FORWARD accept: translation and permission are separate verdicts, and LAN bypasses both
questions.explanation: Correct: nat decides where while filter decides whether — LAN success bypasses both, isolating the missing filter half. VPNs, direct binding, and timeout-celebration dodge the two-verdict structure.

questions.question: Every report sentence in a mini-project needs an artefact (pcap line, counter, ping log): unexhibited claims score zero.
questions.explanation: Correct: evaluators mark artefacts, so every sentence needs a pcap line, counter, or log. Memory-based claims score zero regardless of confidence.

questions.question: What is x after x = temps.append(22.4), and what is the fix?
options: x is None, because append mutates in place and returns nothing; call append alone, then use temps
x is the new list, ready for mean(x)
append is broken for floats
x is 22.4, the appended value
questions.answer: x is None, because append mutates in place and returns nothing; call append alone, then use temps
questions.explanation: Correct: in-place methods return nothing, so x is None — call append alone, then use the list. Broken-append and mean-capacity theories blame the wrong call.

questions.question: Indentation marks blocks in Python, so a stray space can end a block or crash the program.
questions.explanation: Correct: alignment is syntax, so stray spaces end blocks or crash programs. Tracebacks name lines with the complaint last — read bottom-up.

questions.question: np.mean(X) on a (100,5) matrix returned one number instead of per-feature means. What was missing?
options: axis=0, because axis names the collapsed dimension and bare mean collapses everything
A transpose before every mean
A Python loop around the call
Larger float precision
questions.answer: axis=0, because axis names the collapsed dimension and bare mean collapses everything
questions.explanation: Correct: axis names the collapsed dimension, so per-column means need axis=0. Transposes, loops, and precision theories dodge the one-word fix.

questions.question: Broadcasting (100,5) with (5,) stretches legally across rows, so silent stretches need shape-print verification.
questions.explanation: Correct: trailing-axis stretching is automatic, so legal-but-unintended stretches corrupt silently while mismatches error loudly. Shape-printing converts silence into evidence.

questions.question: describe() hides the income column that head() shows. What happened?
options: Income became object type from a stray non-numeric, and describe skips non-numerics: dtypes proves it
describe is broken for large files
Income must be deleted as unmodellable
head hallucinates columns
questions.answer: Income became object type from a stray non-numeric, and describe skips non-numerics: dtypes proves it
questions.explanation: Correct: a stray non-numeric makes object type, which describe skips silently — dtypes proves it. Broken-describe and delete-the-column reactions skip the type ritual.

questions.question: Median filling suits skewed columns like income because the median resists outliers that drag the mean.
questions.explanation: Correct: medians resist the outliers that drag means, so skewed columns take median. Symmetric-only rules and native-NaN myths ignore the describe verdict.

questions.question: A residual plot shows a clear U-curve. What does it confess and what cures it?
options: Systematic underfit from missing bend: add capacity such as polynomial features and confirm flattening on held-out residuals
Perfect fit with decorative curves
Overfitting cured by harder regularisation
More same-kind data fixes any curve
questions.answer: Systematic underfit from missing bend: add capacity such as polynomial features and confirm flattening on held-out residuals
questions.explanation: Correct: U-curves confess missing bend, so capacity (not data volume or regularisation) is the cure, confirmed by flattening held-out residuals. Perfection and overfit readings invert the shape language.

questions.question: A 20k-row scatter renders as one black rectangle unless dots shrink and transparency encodes density.
questions.explanation: Correct: finite ink forces small dots plus alpha so overlaps accumulate into visible density. Deletion and bigger-dot fixes destroy the information the blob hides.

questions.question: Test R-squared is 0.91 but fresh-district data scores 0.62 after full-data scaler fitting. Why?
options: Test statistics leaked into training features, inflating held-out scores that collapse on truly unseen data
Fresh districts are always harder; nothing is wrong
R-squared was computed wrong arithmetically
Scaling is unnecessary for regression
questions.answer: Test statistics leaked into training features, inflating held-out scores that collapse on truly unseen data
questions.explanation: Correct: full-data scaling laundered test statistics into training, inflating scores that collapse on truly unseen distributions. Hardness and arithmetic-error theories skip the leak chain.

questions.question: Pinning random_state makes splits repeatable, so grades reproduce instead of wandering per run.
questions.explanation: Correct: pinned shuffles reproduce, so grades become evidence instead of luck. Training-boost and magic-number theories mistake repeatability for performance.

questions.question: Why must lab scripts read local CSVs instead of fetching datasets from URLs?
options: Offline failure, irreproducibility as remote files change, and wasted minutes per run
URLs are faster than local files
Local files read more slowly
Python forbids URL fetching by law
questions.answer: Offline failure, irreproducibility as remote files change, and wasted minutes per run
questions.explanation: Correct: offline failure, remote mutation, and per-run download minutes each independently kill URL fetching. Speed and legalistic objections miss all three engineering reasons.

questions.question: Recording sklearn versions in every report header turns cross-machine score mysteries into one-line diffs.
questions.explanation: Correct: defaults drift across releases, so version headers turn cross-machine mysteries into one-line diffs. Random-training and hardware-blame theories skip the hidden input.

questions.question: Residuals flatten at predicted 5.0 while truth varies above on housing. Is the model broken?
options: No: targets are censored at the 5.0 cap, so no model can out-predict the ceiling; report the cap and grade the rest
Yes: add wild features to break the ceiling
Yes: remove scaling which clips predictions
R-squared is meaningless on capped data
questions.answer: No: targets are censored at the 5.0 cap, so no model can out-predict the ceiling; report the cap and grade the rest
questions.explanation: Correct: the 5.0 cap censors truth, so no model out-predicts it — report the cap and grade the rest. Feature-chasing and scaler-blame try to fix data facts with model effort.

questions.question: Coefficient importance must be read in standardised units, because raw scales rig apparent sizes.
questions.explanation: Correct: raw scales rig apparent sizes, so importance needs standardised units. Raw-truth and never-measure doctrines defend artefacts as findings.

questions.question: Degree 5 shows train 0.97 with CV 0.71 while degree 2 shows 0.84 with 0.82. Which ships?
options: Degree 2, since the wide train-CV gap of degree 5 confesses memorisation while degree 2 generalises
Degree 5, since train 0.97 is unbeatable
An average of both models
Degree 8 for even higher train scores
questions.answer: Degree 2, since the wide train-CV gap of degree 5 confesses memorisation while degree 2 generalises
questions.explanation: Correct: the wide train-CV gap confesses memorisation while the tight one generalises — ship CV minima. Train-maxima worship and averaging dodge the gap arithmetic.

questions.question: PolynomialFeatures belongs inside the pipeline so every CV fold refits transforms on its own train slice.
questions.explanation: Correct: outside-the-loop transforms leak across folds, so pipelines enforce per-fold honesty. Speed and illegality theories miss the geography of contamination.

questions.question: Lasso keeps AveRooms on one seed but swaps to AveBedrms on another with identical scores. What should the report conclude?
options: Correlated twins share credit unstably: report the swap as correlation evidence, never crown one twin
AveRooms is the true cause; the other seed errored
Lasso is broken for correlated data
Silently average the twins into one feature
questions.answer: Correlated twins share credit unstably: report the swap as correlation evidence, never crown one twin
questions.explanation: Correct: identical scores prove interchangeability, so report the swap as correlation evidence. True-cause crowns and broken-method verdicts overclaim what flips demonstrate.

questions.question: Ridge and Lasso inputs must be standardised because penalties otherwise punish raw magnitudes instead of importance.
questions.explanation: Correct: penalties price magnitudes, so unscaled inputs rig survival by units. Raw-reality and averaging doctrines launder scale artefacts into importance.

questions.question: k=1 scores 100 percent on train but loses cross-validation badly while k=15 tops it. Why?
options: k=1 memorises with huge variance while k=15 smooths neighbourhoods: CV ranks generalisation, train ranks memory
k=1 is the best model and CV is broken
Larger k always wins universally
Variance does not apply to lazy learners
questions.answer: k=1 memorises with huge variance while k=15 smooths neighbourhoods: CV ranks generalisation, train ranks memory
questions.explanation: Correct: k=1 memorises with huge variance while k=15 smooths — CV ranks generalisation, train ranks memory. Universally-larger-k and variance-exemption theories skip the capacity reversal.

questions.question: Comparing classifiers requires identical scaled inputs, splits and seeds, or the ranking is void.
questions.explanation: Correct: shared inputs, splits, and seeds make rankings comparable; rigged races are void results. Partial-scaling and protocol-free comparisons skip comparability itself.

questions.question: For illness screening on 95/5 data, model A has accuracy 0.97 with recall 0.40 while B has 0.91 with 0.90. Which ships?
options: B, because misses kill and A's accuracy is a majority echo while B catches nine of ten sick
A, because accuracy decides everything
Neither without 1.00 recall
Both equally above 0.90
questions.answer: B, because misses kill and A's accuracy is a majority echo while B catches nine of ten sick
questions.explanation: Correct: misses kill in screening, so recall headlines while majority-echo accuracy footnotes. Accuracy-absolutism and 1.00-or-bust demands ignore cost.

questions.question: AUC grades ranking across thresholds, so the deployed dot still needs its own precision and recall report.
questions.explanation: Correct: areas rank across thresholds while dots decide deployments — report both, ship the dot. AUC-equals-precision confusions collapse two different grades.

questions.question: k=7 gives the lowest WCSS on a sweep. Why is k=7 the wrong pick?
options: WCSS falls monotonically with k, so minimising it always over-clusters; pick by elbow kink confirmed by silhouette peak
Lowest WCSS defines the best clustering
WCSS rises with k, making minima meaningful
k must equal the feature count
questions.answer: WCSS falls monotonically with k, so minimising it always over-clusters; pick by elbow kink confirmed by silhouette peak
questions.explanation: Correct: monotone WCSS always over-clusters at the minimum, so elbow kink plus silhouette peak decide. Minimum-worship and feature-count rules misuse the metric.

questions.question: k-means distances must use scaled features, because raw units rig geometry toward large-numbered columns.
questions.explanation: Correct: Euclidean sums eat units, so unscaled geometry reports currency instead of customers. Raw-truth and equal-validity doctrines defend unit-stuffing.

questions.question: Single linkage chains stragglers while complete linkage balls up on the same data. Which is correct?
options: Neither absolutely: linkages favour shapes, so choose by shape hypothesis and report both
Single linkage, since chains are always truer
Complete linkage, since balance is always truer
The data is broken and must be resampled
questions.answer: Neither absolutely: linkages favour shapes, so choose by shape hypothesis and report both
questions.explanation: Correct: linkages favour shapes, so same-data disagreement proves method shapes findings — choose by hypothesis, report both. Always-truer and broken-data verdicts skip the lens effect.

questions.question: Hierarchical clustering defers k because one run records every granularity as dendrogram heights for later cutting.
questions.explanation: Correct: one agglomerative run records every granularity as heights for later cutting, while flat runs hold one resolution. Auto-k and magic theories skip the structural difference.

questions.question: Boosting peaks at 120 rounds then sags by 500 while forests plateau. What ships?
options: About 120 rounds, since peaks ship and endpoints don't: over-rounding memorises noise
500 rounds, since more is more
Forests are obsolete wherever boosting exists
OOB scores should be ignored
questions.answer: About 120 rounds, since peaks ship and endpoints don't: over-rounding memorises noise
questions.explanation: Correct: forests plateau (stop paying) while boosting peaks then sags (stop rounding) — ship validation extrema. More-is-more and OOB-dismissal skip both stop rules.

questions.question: Bagging averages variance while boosting chases bias, so committees need the disease matched to the cure.
questions.explanation: Correct: variance down, then bias down, then noise up — read all three deltas off the staged curve. Always-boost and forests-fix-bias doctrines compress distinct mechanisms.

questions.question: An evaluator reruns a capstone and one stage score differs by 0.02. What decides pass or fail?
options: The recorded stack versions: same code plus same data must match, and the version log convicts or acquits environment drift in one line
Any difference voids everything
Scores don't matter in projects
Rerun until it matches, then present
questions.answer: The recorded stack versions: same code plus same data must match, and the version log convicts or acquits environment drift in one line
questions.explanation: Correct: same code plus same data must match given the recorded stack, and version logs convict environment drift in one line. Any-difference-voids and rerun-till-match dodge conditional reproducibility.

questions.question: Every report sentence in a mini-project needs an artefact behind it, because evaluators mark artefacts, not memories.
questions.explanation: Correct: evaluators mark artefacts, so superlatives need slices with numbers. Decimal-adding and optional-limits attitudes replace evidence with adjectives.

questions.question: A classmate studies only Tarangam guide pages for the MOOC proctored exam. What is wrong?
options: The guides teach navigation, not constitutional content: the exam tests the external MOOC's material
Guides equal courses, so nothing is wrong
MOOCs never hold exams
Guides are banned from citation anywhere
questions.answer: The guides teach navigation, not constitutional content: the exam tests the external MOOC's material
questions.explanation: Correct: guides teach navigation while exams test external content — studying the fixture list never prepares the match. Equivalence and exam-free-MOOC theories collapse the boundary.

questions.question: The approved MOOC listing must be verified with the department each session, since sessions rotate.
questions.explanation: Correct: sessions rotate listings and timelines, so currency is verified per session. Virus and link-ban theories invent dangers while missing the real one.

questions.question: All videos watched in the final weekend, yet completion fails. What went wrong?
options: Graded items with deadlines were missed: views alone rarely satisfy completion
Videos do not count as learning scientifically
Weekends are banned on MOOC platforms
Completion is random and blameless
questions.answer: Graded items with deadlines were missed: views alone rarely satisfy completion
questions.explanation: Correct: completion means graded artefacts on time, not hours watched — bingeing converts watching into regret. Anti-video and randomness theories skip the artefact economy.

questions.question: Posting quiz answers for peers is platform malpractice; concept discussion teaches without copying.
questions.explanation: Correct: posted answers are malpractice up to disqualification; concept discussion teaches cleanly. Read-only and nobody-reads excuses dissolve the integrity boundary.

questions.question: Certificate earned but no credit recorded, with nothing ever submitted to the department. What broke?
options: The submission step: credit needs the notified handoff with acknowledgment
Certificates auto-transfer, so the office erred
Certificates are decorative and worthless
Departments reject all MOOCs on principle
questions.answer: The submission step: credit needs the notified handoff with acknowledgment
questions.explanation: Correct: enroll, progress, certificate, submit, record — unfiled evidence is absent evidence. Auto-transfer and rejection doctrines skip the handoff link.

questions.question: Certificates must match institutional records character-for-character at enrollment, or verification orphans them.
questions.explanation: Correct: corrections later are slow or impossible, so records must match character-for-character at enrollment. Hope-based enrollment defers an unfixable failure.

questions.question: Senior notes disagree with the MOOC transcript on an article's content. Which wins?
options: The official transcript and the constitutional text it cites: verify-then-memorise
Senior notes, since seniors never err
The newer document regardless of source
Both are equally valid
questions.answer: The official transcript and the constitutional text it cites: verify-then-memorise
questions.explanation: Correct: authority resolves upward — constitution, then official material, then everything else. Seniority, novelty, and false-equivalence rules pick the wrong winner.

questions.question: Revision must map to the MOOC's stated week-outcomes because outcomes are the exam's blueprint.
questions.explanation: Correct: outcomes blueprint what is testable, so mapping converts hours into coverage. Decorative-outcome and rewatch-everything doctrines waste effort blindly.
